analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal minimum wage, leaving wage floors entirely to states and cities.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal minimum wage never got a vote; it died in a House subcommittee with 26 Republican backers and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the federal minimum wage by repealing the core wage provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 [S2][S3]. It would also bar the federal government from interfering with state or city minimum wage laws, so any wage floor would depend entirely on where a worker lives [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced in May 1996, sent to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee, referred to a subcommittee, and never advanced to a vote before Congress ended in January 1997 [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage industries — would have been free to pay less than the current federal floor, lowering their labor costs. Workers in states without their own minimum wage laws would have had no federal protection at all.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections of the Fair Labor Standards Act that establish and enforce the federal minimum wage, eliminating the national wage floor [S2][S3].
Prohibits the federal government from regulating or impeding state and local minimum wage laws, leaving the field to states and cities [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Minimum-wage workers, especially in states that do not set their own wage floors, would bear the cost through lower or unchanged pay. Higher-wage workers and regions with strong state wage laws would be less affected.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the federal floor would leave workers' wages dependent on their state: a worker doing the same job would earn a different minimum depending on geography, and states without minimum wage laws would have no floor at all [S2][S3].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that a national wage floor can price some entry-level workers out of jobs and that states are better positioned to set wages suited to local economies; the bill's state-and-local language reflects that view [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs almost entirely to employers through lower labor costs, while its cost falls on the lowest-paid workers, who would lose the national guarantee of a wage floor. Because it would replace one uniform federal standard with a patchwork that many states would not fill in, the costs to workers outweigh the flexibility argument for anyone earning near the minimum.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1996 and sent to a House committee, then to a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Lightfoot introduced the bill on May 16, 1996, joined by 25 Republican cosponsors; all 26 backers were Republicans [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction [S5].
On June 7, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained with no further action [S5].
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without ever reaching the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minimum-wage workers are better off because the bill died; they kept the federal wage floor that it would have erased. Employers hoping to pay below the federal minimum gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage workers who kept the wage floor

for.name: Rep. Jim Lightfoot
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the federal minimum wage

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities / Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referring it to subcommittee; no markup, no floor vote

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Let the bill sit in subcommittee without bringing it up; the committee took no action in the months before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat backed the bill [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Employers of minimum-wage workers (restaurants, retail, other low-wage service businesses)
industries.note: If enacted, the bill would have let these employers pay below the federal minimum, cutting their labor costs at the direct expense of their lowest-paid employees. The bill died, so no gain occurred.

The bill would have barred federal interference with state and city minimum wage laws, giving governments that choose higher wage floors clearer room to act. But it would also have removed the federal floor that backstops states without their own laws.
